utterances.text: As far as I can recall and given that I saw a person from my home town and I knew that he was an active-duty police officer, it was the Serbian police of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You already mentioned, when you were asked by the Judges, the name Simatovic. Do you remember that he came visit you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came to visit us at Pajzos. That was the second part of our training. He didn't come to Lezimir, or at least I didn't see him there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember what he told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at Pajzos I remember that he said that we would be going to Bosnia, that we would be stationed in Bosanski Samac, or, rather, in a village near Bosanski Samac, that we would receive our orders en route as we went by. And he asked if anyone needed any equipment or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did he tell you that it would be a difficult situation in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, he said it would be difficult, because we flew there by helicopter. We couldn't get there by bus, so we had to fly to a village near Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember who provided the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the Yugoslav Army. The pilots were active-duty servicemen, and the helicopters had their insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember if a representative from Bosanski Samac arrived the day when Simatovic visited you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember at least one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Stevan Todorovic. Stevan Todorovic. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you were transported by helicopter to which village; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, it was called Batkusa or something like that. I think it was Batkusa. We landed on the football pitch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember names of persons who were with you in the helicopter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I remember just a couple of names; at least some of them were killed. A few names. I may recall some nicknames. But I'm really bad about names. But I might be able to remember some names, maybe -- well, I do remember the names of people I socialised with, but that's a different story.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember the colour of the berets some of these people were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What people?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The people in the helicopter. Were there people who were wearing red berets, for example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no people with red berets in the helicopter because all of us had camouflage hats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You are sure about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you explain us or tell us who a man with the nickname Crni was, or was it his real name? I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Crni was not in my helicopter. Crni was in the first helicopter. I was in the third one. You asked me if there were any people with red berets in my helicopter, and I said no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Isn't it possible that people like Crni, Mali Vuk [phoen], and Debeli wore red berets on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was your task when you arrived in Batkusa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing at first. We were billeted there. The first couple of days it was physical training, familiarisation with the ground, with members of the reservists or members of the Army of Yugoslavia and local reservists. We got to know the area. Nothing major.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened the night or the evening before the attack on Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the eve of the attack on Bosanski Samac, we had a meeting to negotiate -- to discuss the plan. We were told what to do, how to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who was in command or who was the main person who instructed you? Do you remember the name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember the name, but I remember his nickname, Kriger. He was lieutenant-colonel, if I'm not mistaken. And he was the member of that tactical group, a member of the Yugoslav People's Army. And he was in charge of that part of the territory around Bosanski Samac, the area from Loncari or Gorica; I'm not sure. Pelagicevo as well. That part of the area was under the control of the 17th Tactical Group and local reservists who hailed from the territory, and we were also subordinated to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is it correct when we say that Kriger was the overall commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you now explain us what was the task of your group for the attack on Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was personally tasked with taking the culture hall in Bosanski Samac. Debeli, if I'm not mistaken, was charged with the police station, and he was wounded there. I don't know about the other groups, which group had what task, but I know that there was ones that were sent to the silo, one to the bridge. And that was about all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you find any resistance while you were trying to secure the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was some resistance at the police station. I personally entered the culture hall with an escort without any problems, no resistance there. There was some resistance at the police station, and that's how Debeli got wounded as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember if also a group of locals participated in the liberation of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. There was a group of some 10 or 12 local lads who had undergone training in Pajzos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So you already knew them from that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I knew them by sight. I didn't know them personally. We used to see them around, but just in passing. We never communicated with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did your unit have to fight while securing or attacking the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. There was no resistance to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was the door opened for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a man with a key inside, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And this man opened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you stay all the time in the building or have you been replaced later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Until the morning, until perhaps 10.00 or 11.00, let's say that I and my group stayed in the building until 10.00, and then we were replaced. I can't remember who replaced us. I believe that they were locals or Territorial Defence members who were -- who had arrived later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Were you then told to go to another building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Then we had a short break. Across the street from the SUP building there was a building which housed the Territorial Defence and the civilian protection, or I don't know what the names were at the time. That's where we stayed an hour or two, and there was no pending task for us. We took a short break because we hadn't slept for the entire night and the best part of that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know who was occupying the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that Debeli and his group were tasked with taking the SUP building, and that's where he was wounded, as I've just told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did also a person with a nickname Lugar participate in this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you explain who Lugar was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was from Kragujevac. That's where he was born. That's where he resided and worked. I knew him only briefly. What I knew about him was from the unit. We had some contacts. We used to see each other. He has died in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if he was a member of the SRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: From where; do you know? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Really, I can't. I don't know. Perhaps it was him -- I don't know whether we touched upon the subject or not. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I would -- I would like to show on the monitor the document with the ERN 07530.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Mussemeyer, could we have the 65 ter number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: That is the 65 ter number -- sorry, the exact 65 ter number is 0341-7948.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And could I please see the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you see the picture in the middle of this newspaper article?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That's the late Lugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you read the third paragraph of this article which starts with the words "Miljkovic went to the front as early as 1991 ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could the letters please be blown up? My sight is not very good. Hold on. I have a magnifying glass here. Maybe that will help. The third paragraph, where is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: No. The paragraph which starts with the word "Miljkovic went to the front as early as 1991 ..." It might also be the second paragraph; it depends how you count.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, we must go to the left side of the picture and then -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And there it starts with: "Miljkovic went to the front ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can I propose that I read it in English and the witness will tell us if it is correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Please -- Mr. Witness, please check if what I read from the translation is correct with what is written there. "Miljkovic went to the front as early as 1991, and in speaking of it later on he said: 'My brother was mobilised. When they were cut off between Tovarnik and Ilici, they told me here in the army that the unit did not exist.'" And there are three points. It says: "I asked Vojislav Seselj whether he accepted volunteers and whether people wanted to go to Slavonia, and then I went as a member of the Serbian Radical Party." Is this correct, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand. Are you asking me whether that's what it says here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Exactly, because I read it in English and you can check the original.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So from this article we can conclude that this Lugar asked Mr. Seselj if he can go as an SRS volunteer to the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Although you allowed Mr. Mussemeyer to ask leading questions, this was not a leading question. This was sheer impertinence. One could conclude from this whether Lugar stated for the newspapers or whether the newspapers published that he had stated that he had asked Vojislav Seselj. This is as if I was there at everybody's disposal in Kragujevac for him to ask me. And now Mussemeyer is suggesting to the witness that it can be concluded that indeed he asked me whether he can go. This is impertinent. The witness can only say that this is what he read in the newspapers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is something that I've just read.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there you go. You cannot ask the witness whether this is correct and whether this is a conclusion we can draw. We cannot draw conclusions from a newspaper, can we? There is a statement by Tomislav Nikolic. Nikolic says that Lugar went of his own will in the same article and Nikolic didn't lie. This article was published in 1998. He would probably lie today about this article, about -- like this about anything else. In 1998 he still didn't have the reason to be afraid of The Hague Tribunal. Look at the last paragraph in this column. And this is really very problematic on the part of Mr. Mussemeyer. He is here to establish the truth as an officer of international justice instead of using lies and deceptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your comment is on the transcript. Now, before the break, Mr. Mussemeyer, please put your question to the witness with -- so that -- Bosanski Samac is mentioned in the indictment as a settlement where crimes were committed but crimes that are not blamed on the accused. It was just there to illustrate the consistent pattern of conduct. So put your question now. What do you want to elicit from this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I think the witness already answered this, Your Honour. I asked him if he knows that Lugar was a member of the SRS, and he affirmed this. And then I showed him this newspaper article which is more or less the same, what he has already testified about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, you said that Lugar had been a volunteer of the SRS. Very well. Now, I would like to know the following: I would like to know whether -- when exactly occurred the operation on Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm not mistaken - and I believe I'm not - I remember the date. It was on the 17th of April, or, rather, during the night between the 16th and the 17th of April, if I'm not mistaken. I repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992. In your statement on paragraph 52 - let me refresh your memory - you said that Lugar's Group was under VRS command. Did you say this, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you are referring to as Lugar's Group, that doesn't have anything to do with the 17 of April. It could not be put in connection with the 17th of April. It was much later. Lugar had his own group; he arrived with his own group after my arrival from hospital, and I arrived from hospital sometime in mid-June. And then the unit returned to Serbia. And perhaps some ten days later Lugar came with a group of volunteers and then he was a volunteer. Up to that moment, he was not a volunteer. Lugar was not a volunteer. He was the commander of the first squad in the battle group Samac. And he was under the JNA command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I understand from this that all operations conducted were conducted under JNA command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that moment up to the 17th of May, 1992, the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then after which command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... as I have read it here, it was the 2nd Posavina Brigade. I don't know the exact name of the unit. After that, it was under the command of the Army of Republika Srpska or whatever it was called at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now, an essential question for me and I believe for my fellow Judges also: I would like to know, when these military operations occurred, all these military operations of all sorts, were they always under -- were they under direct command of the SRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What operations? I did not understand the gist of your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For example, the operation on Bosanski Samac. I would like to know whether this operation was conducted under the command of the SRS.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... operation -- at that time there were no volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party in Bosanski Samac and its environs; only the army and our unit that had arrived by helicopters. You couldn't travel through Bijeljina or Brcko because the roads was impassable at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Bosanski Samac was a military operation conducted by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know whether there were SRS volunteers among the troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Among the troops? You mean the JNA? The army that we found there? I don't know if there were any volunteers. There were soldiers. The way I saw things and whatever soldiers I met, I don't know if there were any volunteers. They all bore the insignia of the then-Yugoslav People's Army. I don't know if there were any volunteers. I wouldn't be able to tell you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We must break now because the tape is almost over. We'll have a 20-minute break. And let me remind Mr. Mussemeyer that he has about 30 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Mr. Mussemeyer, you have something like 30 minutes left, no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I'll try to do it in this time, Your Honour. Mr. Registrar, could you please call up on the monitor the document which has the 65 ter number 1724. This is a document which has already been admitted recently on the 17th of February, 2010, and it has the P number 01018. This is Official Notes from questioning of the accused Slobodan Miljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I know that you don't have the best eye - sorry - for this, but could I ask you to go on the first page in to the middle and read who is present. This is a record of questioning of accused. Now, you can see an investigating judge, a recording clerk, and the accused. Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's on the right-hand side of this document, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Exactly. What do you read as the name of the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Slobodan Miljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And this Slobodan Miljkovic is the person who has the nickname Lugar; can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could we go to page 3 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Witness, there is what is for me is interesting what is written in paragraph 7 of this document which starts: "I was the commander of the special purpose group ..." Sorry, your -- it starts with: "Before my arrival at the front line in Bosanska Posavina, I was in eastern Slavonia ..." Can you follow what I'm reading slowly in English that it is correct on the B/C/S version? I start again at paragraph 7: "Before my arrival at the front lines in Bosanska Posavina, I was in eastern Slavonia, where I spent a while working in the police. I was even deputy commander of the police station in Koprivna village. After that we went to train to Pajzos and Lezimir, and after the training we were transferred by helicopter to Batkusa village in Bosanska Posavina. Before going to Posavina, there were contacts with the Samac public security station chief, Stevan Todorovic, and the agreement was made for a group of Radicals to come to assist the soldiers in Posavina. Our first operation occurred seven to eight days after we arrived in Posavina. The operation was aimed at the town of Samac, which we liberated in 38 minutes. I was commander of the special purpose unit at the time." Is it correct what is written there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In part. I don't know how this was translated and who did the translation, but, at that time, Slobodan was the commander, "komandir," of the first squad. And the unit commander was Srecko Debeli, "komandant." Crni and Vuk were in charge of maintaining radio contact with Serbia, and that's all. And half of the things quoted here are not correct. I don't know whether he stated there -- that there or not. I'm not going to go into that. But he was a squad commander, squad leader. He did not command the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What is interesting for me is - I ask you if you can confirm this - if Stevan Todorovic asked for a group of Radicals to be sent to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. I can't say that. But a group of Radicals was not sent to Bosanski Samac at all. It was not a group of Radicals that went by helicopter there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one brief objection. Mr. Mussemeyer has a statement by Stevan Todorovic, and he also has Simo Zaric's statement; He was also tried here. Stevan Todorovic had a plea bargain with the Prosecution. They testify about an agreement with Lugar's Group sometime in autumn of that year where they asked for a large sum of money in order to get involved there, but it couldn't have been in May when this group became part of the 17th Tactical Group of the JNA. So the Prosecution has that, and they can use it. They have Simo Zaric's statement and Stevan Todorovic's statement, and they didn't give me any of those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you are saying now is typically something you could have asked during your cross-examination. Please proceed, Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Before I come to the events in Crkvina, I would like you to admit the newspaper article, which we were using before, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this not already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Not the newspaper article. This statement of Lugar was admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, the press article, could we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that will be Exhibit P1041.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I would like to come to the events which happened obviously in Crkvina. Can you tell us what happened there in May 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have said in my statement, several people were killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Please let us now how you were involved. Were you present at that time? How did you come to this event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was present there on that day, if I'm not mistaken. We said farewell to Vuk Vukovic -- I don't know if that was his last name. Vuk was his nickname. Maybe I went on a furlough by car. I was in a restaurant; I sat down to eat something. And then I wanted to go back to the camp. And then I went to Crkvina. Upon Lugar's invitation, I went to the crossroads where the prisoners were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What did Lugar tell you what he has to do there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Lugar said that he had been given an order and that he had to do something there. I didn't know what it was all about. I headed there. He commanded a squad, and I, myself, I was the commander of the third squad, so there was no reason for me not to accompany him, given that he had asked me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Where did you go, you and Lugar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several of us. He was alone; he had his escort. And we went to Crkvina, to that place where the prisoners were located. It was a hall of some sort. It was already dark, if I'm not mistaken. It was in the evening -- in fact, I'm sure it was in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Where were these prisoners held prisoner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the hangar, a hall of some sort. I don't know what its original purpose was. But at any rate it was an empty room perhaps the size of this courtroom, slightly longer perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What did Lugar do then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a conflict, gun-fire. I left the place. I went out. I don't know what happened later. I didn't see what happened. Later on, I heard that several people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you see the prisoners in the barn?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember how many it were approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, 20, 30; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did Lugar order something to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't recall. I don't think that there was any need to do that. They all got up the moment the door opened and the moment we got in. They all got up. They just stood there. I don't recall him ordering anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Had they to be lined up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was usual procedure for them to line up. It was normal -- well, normal. It was the usual thing to do, to get up and to line up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did they do this automatically or have they been asked to do this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that they immediately started getting up. I'm not sure, but I think that they started getting up the moment the door opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And then they lined up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What did Lugar do the next moments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. There was an altercation, threats, weapons were pulled, and I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard several shots. I didn't know if they were fired in the air or if they were fired at people. Later on I heard that several people had been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can I refresh the witness's memory because he is departing a bit from his former statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you said in your statement in paragraph 46: "We went to Crkvina, where I observed about 30 to 35 men dressed in civilian clothes lined up along two walls. I then observed when Lugar," and there is a second man, I will ask you the name later, "fired on these men, killing five to seven of them. I'm not sure if Debeli also participated in the execution of these people, but he was present." Do you remember having said this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, Debeli is not Srecko Radovanovic. Let us make that clear. There was another man called Debeli, precisely because he was fat, that's what it means in Serbian; and secondly, I never stated that Lugar fired shots at anyone. When I was asked whether Lugar -- or, rather, I remember that I said I would not make any comments about my comrade, and that should have been recorded. I never said I saw Lugar shoot anyone, and I didn't say that I actually saw the shooting. I never saw any of the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember a person with a nickname Tralja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you sure that you never said that Lugar and Tralja fired on these men, killing five to seven?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sure that I didn't say that they fired their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: But you signed a statement like this, aren't you -- didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I signed each and every statement that I gave, but I'm sure that I never said that because that is not true. Because I know that people were tried for this incident, and probably you yourself made those conclusions. I was not called to testify at that trial, but I know what I said. To one of your investigators I actually invoked my right not to speak about that, and that should have been recorded here. I said I didn't want to speak about that. And once he started probing me about details, I said, "I'm sorry. I don't want to discuss it." Because, once again, I feel very uncomfortable here mentioning a person who cannot defend himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you are saying that there was a trial. Who was convicted at this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I know -- I saw it on TV, that somebody was tried for the Crkvina crime, but who was convicted? I really don't know. I just saw it on TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The investigating judge did not ask you to take the stand as a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would like to show the witness now his two statements he has given and signed and will put some questions to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, this is your -- the first statement you gave in April 2004, obviously. Could you have a look on this -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, the witness did not sign that statement -- or at least I don't have his signature on the copy that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 2004 statement which is the copy I have bears his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you have a copy in English, but you know that I'm not interested in this revolting language at all. The Serbian language is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The English language is a repulsive language, why do you say that? That is not very useful. Whatever the case may be, we have a document which is signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Judge, imagine me signing something in Japanese, Chinese, or Arabic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is why I asked him whether he was conversant in English. And he said he was; he could read and understand it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be given the paragraph that you want me to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: No, I don't want to read -- that you read any paragraph. Could you please have a look on the first page of this statement. Could you turn the page. Do you see somewhere your signature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Each and every page is signed by me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is it the same with the second statement you gave? Could you please check. Is it correct that each page has your signature?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will have to redact this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I may have made a mistake here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session. Registrar, please, we must redact this instantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's my statement. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please go to page 18 of your second statement and read the witness acknowledgement there. It's the last page, I guess, or the page before the last page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The last --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you read the witness acknowledgement there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read the statement in the Serbian language, and it contains everything I said to the best of my knowledge and recollection. I have given the statement voluntarily, and I am aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal -- yes, I'm sorry. I apologise. "I have given this statement voluntarily, and I am aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the international criminal tribunal for the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991 and that I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is there a signature at the right-hand at the bottom of this acknowledgement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you signed, on 20 September 2006, this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I can't recall the date. It's probably correct, but that's the statement that I signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have an additional question to this. Weren't you told at the 20th of September that this statement is taken for the Seselj case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no. If I may, I was told -- and in each and every one of my statements perhaps there are two or three pages that relate to 1991. I answered the questions that pertained to 1992, and at that time I had nothing to do with the Radical Party apart from coming across the some volunteers from time to time and apart from the fact that some of the members of my unit were Serbian Radical Party volunteers. But it is immaterial whether I was told or not that I would be testifying at the Vojislav Seselj trial. I'm telling you what I know. It doesn't matter in which case I'm testifying. But I never was told that I would come here to testify in his case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can I ask --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- that wouldn't have changed anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: -- can I ask an additional question. Please go to paragraph 61 of your statement, which is maybe on page 18 of your version, and read the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read the statement in the Serbian language. It contains everything that I said to the best of my knowledge and recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I refer to paragraph 61, which has the number 61 before. No, you must go a page before and there are paragraph numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 61, page 16. 61: "Based on my experience as a CRS [as interpreted] volunteer in both Croatia and Bosnia, the CRS as a party and particularly Seselj were very popular. Many SRS volunteers, i.e., volunteers, considered that sacrifices they were making were part of the fight for the Serbian people and the objective instrumental to the creation of a Greater Serbia. They firmly believed in the political agenda and rhetoric furnished by Seselj." Again, something that is only partially true. I was a volunteer of the SRS also in Bosnia; however, that was in 1995 on Majevica Mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: But you said in the first sentence that you were an SRS volunteer in both Croatia and Bosnia; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, and I was. I never denied that. But I was a volunteer of the SRS in 1995, in -- on Mount Majevica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. Can you please tell us if you have given an additional statement to other parties of this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What statements?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you put your question again slower, Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I want to know from the witness if he gave another statement to the Defence in December 2007.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I think we might go into closed session if he wants to develop or explain us how it came to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me consult with my fellow Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You can ask your question for 2007. Are we in private session? Mr. Registrar, could we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe you have four minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I request orally that the two statements the witness gave to the OTP on 22nd of April, 2004, and 20 of September, 2006, are admitted into evidence. The witness departed substantially in many details from his former statement, and I think the statement -- the facts he described in the OTP statements are the truth and what he told us today for many details I cannot believe it. This is my -- the end of my cross -- of my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I absolutely contest that. I object. It is impossible for this to be tendered into evidence. Rule 92 quinquies cannot be applied in my proceedings because it was adopted late last year. And you know what my position is on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, Mr. Seselj, the Trial Chamber will rule after the cross-examination. So as of now we do not rule on anything. We have 15 minutes left. You may start with your cross-examination because we're going to be running late. As you know, we have another witness scheduled for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Sorry, before Mr. Seselj can start, I have a short observation. Like usual, we got his documents only at the last break. They are all in B/C/S. And there is no reason that he could have [sic] tendered this before because they come from 1991 and also some of them from 2008. So he could have provided these documents much earlier, that we could at least prepare for the cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, as always Mr. Mussemeyer doesn't know what he's talking about. The third document that you received is a photocopy of the entire issue of the paper "Great Serbia" dating back from 1991. I know with certainty that the OTP photocopied all of the issues of Greater Serbia in the National Library of Serbia and that they have those at their disposal. What I have provided today is just by way of advising the OTP that I'm going to use it, and they have everything at their disposal, not only this issue but all the issues of that newspaper. Second of all, there are two statements that I'm going to use in cross-examination. I'm not going to tender them. Please don't make me waste time on that. Let me start my cross-examination. If we are left with some time tomorrow after the second witness, then you can present procedural objections and open procedural issues. Let me not do that today. When we had the last witness or the witness before that, I was denied one part of the time for my cross-examination because of the procedural questions. I would like to start. May I, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Mr. VS-1058, do you have your 2004 statement before you in English? In English, please. The one that you signed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could you please turn to page 12. Have you got it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please bear with me just for a moment. I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Is that in English as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Could you please read paragraph 46. Could you please read it in English, and I would kindly ask the interpreter to -- not to interpret that paragraph into either Serbian or French. We would like -- I would like the Judges to hear how you read English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, 46. Could you please read it in English. On page 12, that is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 46 is on page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It may be on page 9 in the English version. If it is, please read it in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. [In English] "Sometime in early May 1992 I was present in Crkvina when five to seven men were executed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must say that the witness had told us that he understood English well, but he had some problem speaking English, probably pronouncing and reading English. We're not going to ask this witness to pass an English exam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to translate what I've just read?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you don't allow me this question, I would kindly ask you, Mrs. Lattanzi, and I will continue my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did not put any question, Mr. Seselj. How could I tell you that you should not put any question to witness? You didn't put any question to him. You only asked him to read out loud something in English, part of his statement. Now, what's the question? Put the question, and we'll see. We want a question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that you're curious what the question was going to be. I am not going to put it to the witness because you didn't allow the witness to read the whole paragraph, so I'm going to deny you the pleasure of satisfying your curiosity. I'm not going to ask the question. That's how I decided I'm going to ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Excuse me, before we move on, the record is incomplete because the witness read out a sentence from the statement. The sentence is correctly transcribed, but the record does not reflect how the witness actually read out the statement. And it should be put on record that the witness read out the sentence correctly and without hesitation. And he has actually show that he is fully capable of reading and understanding English. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is true that the witness read the paragraph in English, seemingly without any problems. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, the paragraph has not been read out. Only one sentence has been read out in a rather poor English. The paragraph has not been read out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... right. His English is probably not as good as yours, for sure, but still --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Much worse than mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He read the beginning of this paragraph. You're right. He only read the beginning of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my English, although better than his, is not good enough for me to be able to use it in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. VS-1058, let's go back to the year 1991. You remember that at that time Franjo Tudjman came into power in Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Tudjman revive all the Ustasha symbols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Ustasha emigrants start to come back in droves to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that the time of the first initial persecutions of the Serbian population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were Serbs fired if they did not sign the statement of loyalty to the regime of Tudjman at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did refugees from Croatian cities start coming to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Croatian policemen start threatening village population, Serb population, across the Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did that provoke the spontaneous resistance of Serbian population where they were a majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we've already mentioned that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did that happen across the Dalmatia, Lika, Kordun, Banja, western Slavonia, eastern Slavonia, and Baranja?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the new Croatian authorities start encircled the JNA garrisons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please try to slow down. The interpreters are raising the white flag. They're out of breath.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that Tudjman's regime organised wide actions to block JNA barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Tudjman announce that there would be a cessation of Croatia from Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did that disturb the Serb population in the Croatian federal unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the Serbs start organising themselves into village guards in order to protect their homes from attacks by Croatian paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Tudjman himself organise the biggest paramilitary formation that he called the Croatian guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did he carry out a review of that unit in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was in the Dinamo stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Was that unit a legal unit from the aspect of the then-prevailing laws in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did he formally join that unit to his police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did the first killings of Serb civilians happen because Serbs considered them unsuitable for their future state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You heard that Serbian villages in eastern Slavonia started organising barricades at the entrances and that they started keeping guards around-the-clock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: There was -- certain negotiations took place between local Serbs and the Croatian authorities at the time, allegedly with a view to calming down the boiling situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes, that was mentioned on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that the Serbian Radical Party in April 1991 organised the first group of volunteers and sent it to Borovo Selo that was under threat at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I believe so. I believe I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that they, together with the locals, held watches at the access roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you know that an agreement was reached with the Croatian authorities that the Croatian authorities would not send police units into the Serb villages and that the Serbs would lift the roadblocks from the access roads?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that I recall all that, but I think that it did occur like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And do you remember that the Croatian police, together with the armed civilians, including some Kurds, entered Borovo Selo on buses after the roadblocks were lifted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Croatian police officers were the first to open fire and that at the spot in the centre of the village they killed Vojislav Milic, who was not armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I was not present there, but I remember that, yes. I was not present, so I don't know some of the details that you're asking me about. I can't really give you an answer. I was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But all the media reported that the volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party who were billeted in the culture hall then grabbed their weapons and returned fire on the Croatian police officers. You have to recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you remember that a handful of our volunteers managed to repel the attack by more than a hundred Croatian policemen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The population of Borovo Selo was in the field. They were tending to their fields. It was the corn season?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not from the rural area, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when the villagers heard the gun-fire, they grabbed weapons, offered resistance, and then the Croats started demanding an intervention of the JNA, crying and moaning about it. Did all the media report that in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then a tank unit of the JNA came in to put a stop to the clash. Serbs stopped fighting. The JNA helped the Croats pull out their wounded and killed. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It was on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: After that, the Serbian Radical Party started sending its volunteers to a number of Serb villages in eastern Slavonia en masse; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The role of those volunteers was exclusively to defend the Serb villages; am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to keep watch and to assist the villagers and the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The JNA at the time was not involved in the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You were there as a volunteer of the Serbian Radical Party when you first went to the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Together with the group of volunteers that you were part of, you went to Milutina Bojica Street in Belgrade yourself and you stated that in your statements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that's the street name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You went to the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether this was the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party or whether it was just a local chapter of the party, but it was the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Since at that time the state did not provide premises for the opposition parties to ensure their normal work, the Serbian Radical Party was forced to rent an apartment in Milutina Bojica Street and to have its headquarters there. You are not aware of that, are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- well, I know that it had to do with the Serbian Radical Party. There was an office there. I don't know whether it was the central office or a branch office.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes. But this was an office where I went to every day to do my day-to-day business in the party.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I think we will stop now because I have to give a few instructions to this witness. Witness, you're now in the hands of justice because you take a solemn declaration. Come back tomorrow at 2.15, but up until now you're not supposed to contact anyone. Furthermore, I would like to know whether you have a cell phone with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have it with me. It's in the witness room. I do have my mobile phone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me give you a piece of advice. Do not answer your cell phone if it rings because you're not supposed to contact anyone until tomorrow. And tomorrow once your testimony is over, you can call whoever you want. But up until now please stay quiet and avoid any problems. Do you understand me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand, but I cannot use it because my network is useless here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You can't use it. Good news.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I only use it as an alarm clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can use it as an alarm clock.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I use the two minutes left to complete this topic so that we don't waste any time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At page 37 of the newspaper, everybody can see that, the Judges and the Prosecution. There is a communique. The headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party has been moved from Milutina Bojica Street number 2 to Marsala Street number 8, and the new telephone number of the party is such and such. So could you please look; that's at page 37 of the photocopy that I provided to you. So in July, late July or maybe -- well, it's a July issue. By July we left Milutina Bojica Street because we finally got a premises from the state in Marsala Birjuzova Street number 58, it was a local commune office, and then we went to the Ohridska Street, the famous Ohridska street. So no party had official premises from the authorities. We all had to rent private accommodation. Once we were granted premises by the state, we left this apartment in Milutina Bojica Street. I think that's evidence enough for you so that the Prosecution can no longer be dealing with some mysterious apartments in Milutina Bojica Street. That used to be the headquarters of the Serbian Radical Party, and we moved out of it in July. So we can complete this topic now, and then I will address other issues tomorrow. That was the reason why I asked all those questions which might have seemed strange at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, we will resume tomorrow at 2.15. I wish you all a pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of March, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
